extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, publishers, eprint server operators, biomedical researchers and authors interested in preprint/peer-review models
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for accepting, moderating, and using electronic preprints (eprints/NetPrints) and for designing sequential or online peer-review processes that combine public comments and commissioned review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly consensus as an evaluation variable
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent of scholarly consensus is an important variable for acceptance; variation in consensus helps explain differing rejection rates across fields and seems likely to be important in readers' and editors' evaluations of eprints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholarly consensus involves shared conceptions of appropriate problems, approaches, and techniques; low consensus leads scholars to view others' work as deficient. Rapid online responses to an eprint might provide a basis for assessing the extent of scholarly consensus. Hargens suggested examining the probability that a published paper will provoke a critical comment as a possible measure of scholarly consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishment of trust
rubrics_metrics.description: "Establishing trust" may be a separate process from initial internet 'publication' of manuscripts and may have many different faces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trust is a crucial aspect of scholarly consensus and affects how eprints are evaluated and accepted over time; systems and signals that help establish trust are important when assessing eprints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial checks / screening for public-health implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Some eprint servers (e.g., The Lancet's) perform editorial checks prior to posting to address concerns that inadequately evaluated eprints with significant public-health implications might cause unnecessary harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eprint servers can include pre-posting editorial screening focused on potential public-health harm; where such checks are applied, they should be explicit and may be part of the acceptance criteria for posting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit labelling that an eprint is not yet peer-reviewed
rubrics_metrics.description: ClinMed NetPrints includes an explicit warning that the eprint has not yet been peer-reviewed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear warnings about peer-review status should be displayed to readers to mitigate misinterpretation and potential harm, especially for clinically relevant content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of unsolicited public comments with commissioned review
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination of unsolicited comments together with commissioned review might yield articles of higher quality than either could accomplish alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While potentially higher-quality, systematically applying both unsolicited public commentary and commissioned review for all eprints would be time-consuming and labor-intensive; selective use or sequential processes may be preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequential review process (proposed model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin with acceptance of a preprint by an eprint server, followed by revision based on public or private comments, and then solicitation of selected eprints for commissioned (conventional) peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sequential approach can act as simultaneous submission to many journals, may benefit authors (especially early-career), create competition among journals, and could lead to higher-quality manuscripts; however, some established journals may resist and practical implementation requires incentives and editorial effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treating posted eprints as equivalent to submissions for editorial solicitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors could regard NetPrints posted at an eprint server as equivalent to articles submitted directly to their journal and, after screening, invite selected authors to submit NetPrints (or revised versions) for conventional peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using eprint servers as a pool for solicitation allows editors to 'dip' into preprints that fit their journal's niche; authors may then choose among invitations—effectively functioning as simultaneous submission across journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: JIME three-stage online peer-review process (gold standard example)
rubrics_metrics.description: JIME's three-stage process: (1) editor-assigned reviewers provide comments in private (accessible to editors, reviewers, authors), (2) revised articles approved by editors are posted publicly as preprints with identified reviewers/readers able to comment, (3) authors prepare a final version accounting for comments for final publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This model includes publicly identified reviewers, posting of reviewer comments and authors' responses, and editorial summaries if comments are numerous. It is resource-intensive and may only be practical for journals with a small number of articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public identification of reviewers and transparency of comments
rubrics_metrics.description: JIME posts reviewers, readers, and editors publicly identified and allows them to post comments; editors may post summaries if comments become numerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency (identifying participants and making comments public) can enrich discourse and accountability, but requires management (e.g., editor summaries) to handle volume and maintain civility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and limits of postpublication (self-selected reader) comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Postpublication review by readers on the internet is no substitute for commissioned prepublication review, but can provide editors with valuable input from individuals who would not otherwise be consulted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-selected comments are valuable supplementary information—useful for detecting issues and broadening input—but should not be relied on as the sole quality-control mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for incentives to elicit reader responses
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of an appropriate incentive (such as a request from a well-respected editor for a peer-review commentary), responses to NetPrints may not be frequent unless the topic is especially controversial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eprint servers and journals should consider mechanisms (editor requests, recognition, moderation, or other incentives) to encourage constructive public commentary; without incentives, public commenting is likely sparse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private solicitation of constructive commentary via colleagues and forums
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors can solicit constructive criticisms privately from respected colleagues or via online discussion groups and forums (example: American Scientist Forum moderated discussions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private or moderated fora can supplement public comments, providing targeted expert feedback that may be more detailed or actionable than general public comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usage statistics as potential quality indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Eprint archives should ideally include standardized, publicly-accessible statistics on usage (e.g., number of visits, number of downloads, median duration of visits) as possible indicators of relative popularity or quality of individual eprints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such statistics may be helpful for evaluative studies but need assessment against conventional quality criteria; repositories could collect and publish consistent metrics to support evaluation research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat about measurement and indicator selection (Tukey warning)
rubrics_metrics.description: "When the right thing can only be measured poorly, it tends to cause the wrong thing to be measured, only because it can be measured well."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious using easily-measured proxies (e.g., download counts) as indicators of quality; choose measures that reflect meaningful attributes and interpret them in context to avoid incentivizing the wrong behaviors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review reform goal: encourage innovation without sacrificing quality control
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review should be reformed in ways that encourage innovation without a sacrifice of quality control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design online and sequential review processes to balance openness and innovation with rigorous assessment—combining selected commissioned review with public commentary may help achieve this balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical constraints: workload and scale limit some online review models
rubrics_metrics.description: Processes like JIME's three-stage model are time-consuming and require a lot of effort; such models are unlikely to be practical unless submission volumes are low.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing review workflows, consider scalability: extensive multi-stage public+commissioned review may be feasible for small, selective journals but not for high-volume pipelines without additional resources or moderation strategies.
